critic.verdict: A purposeful pull-back: it opens tight on the man at the drafting table and steadily reveals the crane, shophouses, crates and cement bags, expressing the scale of the business he is building. The man stays coherent against the table, no tearing, ghosting or awkward edge clipping is visible, the dusty ambient is subtle, and both the tight opening and the full-plate final frame read well in the period silkscreen style.

rounds.verdict: Do not publish: the pull-back idea suits the story, but the opening frame lacks the subject and the entrance creates a transparent ghost through the man.
filmIssues: First frame (t=0) is a poor opening picture: the man is absent because his entrance has not started, leaving an empty drafting table as the hero image.
At t=0.2 the man's rise/fade entrance is a visible transparent ghost — the rooftops and blueprint show through his body, breaking subject coherence and the flat silkscreen print style.

The pull-back reveal itself is apt for nation-building, but the entrance undermines it; the remaining movement is only a modest centred pull-back, no better than a plain camera move once the ghost is removed.

plan.rationale: A quiet turning point becomes a triumph of nation-building: the camera opens tight on the man leaning over his blueprints, he rises in early to take his place at the table, and the reveal travels out to the crane, shophouses, crates and cement bags of the business he is building.

rounds.verdict: A coherent, clean pull-back in intention, but on screen the move is too timid to register as a reveal — it is barely better than a plain static wide and does not yet earn publication.
filmIssues: The intended tight-to-wide pull-back barely reads on the contact sheet: all six frames are essentially the same wide composition, with the man, crates, bags, crane and rooftops already fully visible at t=0. The reveal of the business/nation being built is therefore not visible or purposeful.

The opening frame is a good wide picture but not the promised tight opening on the man leaning over the blueprints; the final frame is almost indistinguishable from it, so the dwell image gains little from the move.
No tearing, doubled edges, halo or ghost is visible around the man, and the layers that belong together stay coherent. No layer clips the frame awkwardly.
Dust is fitting for a construction site and remains subtle, and the 1970s silkscreen/halftone print style is preserved.

plan.rationale: Remove the ghosting entrance so the man is solid and present in the opening frame, tight on him leaning over the blueprints. A clear, purposeful pull-back then reveals the crane, shophouses, crates and cement bags — the business and nation he is building — ending on the full wide plate as the dwell image. Dust stays as a subtle site atmosphere.
